profiles.meeting_scenario: At a tertiary-care hospital, an emergency medicine attending and a clinical pharmacy specialist meet for a 30-minute brainstorming session to generate ideas for updating the emergency department's approach to patients who arrive with markedly elevated blood pressure, in light of newer guidance that emphasizes identifying true hypertensive emergencies through the BARKH framework and moving away from the older 'hypertensive urgency/crisis' language. The agenda is to sketch possible components of a pilot ED pathway, including bedside assessment, medication-selection support, and disposition workflow, without yet committing to a final protocol. The expected outcome is a short list of 3-4 candidate elements to bring to a larger multidisciplinary protocol meeting next week.

members.name: Dr. Elena Ruiz
members.role: Emergency Medicine Attending and ED Clinical Pathway Lead
members.expertise: Acute care triage, ED protocol design, bedside evaluation of cardiovascular emergencies
members.background: Elena has worked in a high-volume urban emergency department for nine years and recently took on a quality-improvement role focused on reducing unnecessary admissions and testing while improving recognition of time-sensitive emergencies.
members.private_state: She wants a pathway that helps residents distinguish true hypertensive emergencies from severe but uncomplicated blood pressure elevations, because she is concerned the current culture still overreacts to the number itself and clogs monitored beds.
hidden_assumptions: A 'symptom-based' pathway should trigger deeper testing only when the history or exam suggests BARKH organ involvement, rather than launching a broad default workup for every severe blood pressure reading.
A 'BARKH screen' is primarily a rapid bedside clinical assessment and documentation prompt, not a bundled set of automatic orders.
An 'observation pathway' refers mainly to ED observation for patients without confirmed end-organ injury who need repeat exams, oral medication adjustment, or blood pressure trend monitoring.
If the team says they are aligning with the new ESC framing, that also implies de-emphasizing legacy triage labels like 'hypertensive urgency' in day-to-day ED workflow.

members.name: Daniel Cho, PharmD
members.role: Clinical Pharmacy Specialist for Cardiology and Critical Care
members.expertise: IV antihypertensive use, medication safety, EHR order-set design, monitored infusion workflows
members.background: Daniel supports the ED, ICU, and cardiology services on high-risk medication use and has led several EHR order-set revisions aimed at reducing treatment delays and standardizing nursing monitoring requirements.
members.private_state: He wants any new pathway to produce safer, more standardized medication ordering and monitoring, and he is especially concerned about ad hoc IV antihypertensive use without enough documentation of target-organ assessment.
hidden_assumptions: A 'symptom-based' pathway still begins from a standard severe-hypertension workup floor, with symptoms mainly determining which medication branch or specialty escalation is chosen.
A 'BARKH screen' is most useful if it is operationalized through the EHR as a structured order-and-documentation bundle that ensures minimum evaluation of each organ domain.
An 'observation pathway' usually means a monitored holding period after IV antihypertensive treatment or infusion initiation, often before ICU or step-down transfer.
The practical starting point for this project is to modify the existing EHR 'hypertensive crisis' build rather than change front-end triage language first.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they want a 'symptom-based algorithm' for severe blood pressure presentations.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means symptoms and bedside findings determine whether broader diagnostic evaluation is initiated at all beyond a limited initial assessment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a baseline workup is still presumed, and symptoms mainly determine which treatment branch, monitoring intensity, or consultant pathway is selected afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds fully aligned because both are reacting against number-driven treatment and both can sincerely describe their approach as 'symptom-based' without noticing that one is talking about the diagnostic boundary and the other about downstream tailoring.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both propose building in a quick 'BARKH screen' early in the ED visit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 envisions a rapid clinician checklist in the note or triage conversation: neuro symptoms, chest pain, dyspnea, oliguria, visual changes, pulse deficits, and focused exam cues that may or may not lead to orders.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 envisions an EHR-supported screening workflow with default labs and tests tied to BARKH domains, such as creatinine, urinalysis, ECG, troponin in selected branches, and prompts for retinal or vascular evaluation documentation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In brainstorming, 'screen' naturally sounds lightweight and early-stage, so neither person feels a need to specify whether it is a cognitive bedside check or an order-set mechanism.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say some patients should go through an 'observation pathway' instead of automatic admission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means patients with severe blood pressure elevation but no confirmed BARKH injury can stay in ED observation for serial exams, repeat blood pressure checks, and medication adjustment before discharge.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means patients with a treated hypertensive emergency can spend a monitored interval under observation protocols while IV medication effects and nursing parameters are stabilized before transfer.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The shared phrase signals sensible bed stewardship to both of them, and because they are brainstorming at a high level, each assumes the other is talking about the same operational bucket when in fact they are imagining different patient populations.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'moving away from urgency/crisis language' practically changes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both endorse 'moving away from hypertensive urgency/crisis language' in the updated approach.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means frontline ED terminology, resident teaching, and disposition thinking should stop using those categories so that severe asymptomatic hypertension is no longer treated as a quasi-emergency.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the conceptual shift can coexist for now with the existing EHR and triage infrastructure labeled 'hypertensive crisis,' with the main immediate change being better medication and assessment guidance inside that framework.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They share the same policy-sounding statement and both cite the new guidance approvingly, but one treats it as a workflow-language reset while the other treats it as a background rationale that does not yet require renaming the operational tools.

turns.inner_thought: What I want is a front-end decision aid that stops residents from spiraling into a full emergency workup just because the blood pressure is 220/120. The newer ESC-style framing gives us cover to stop treating severe asymptomatic hypertension like a pseudo-emergency. If we can get people to use a symptom-based algorithm and move away from hypertensive urgency/crisis language, we can free monitored beds and focus attention on the true BARKH cases.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. From the ED side, I think we really need a cleaner symptom-based algorithm for the patient who rolls in with a very high blood pressure, and the newer guidance gives us a good opening to rethink the whole approach. I’d also love for us to keep moving away from hypertensive urgency or crisis language in how we frame this.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with the conceptual shift, but the practical place to start is still the existing hypertensive crisis build in the EHR. We already have nursing monitoring logic and medication guardrails there; it just needs to be modernized. If we can refresh that build and embed better assessment prompts, we can make IV antihypertensive use safer without waiting for a full front-end nomenclature overhaul.
turns.utterance: I’m with you. It actually feels like a good opportunity to refresh the existing build so the medication pathways are more consistent and safer while we’re updating the clinical framing. We can absolutely move away from the older urgency/crisis language in the updated approach and still make the operational piece stronger.

turns.inner_thought: The first thing should be a quick bedside BARKH screen: symptoms, focused exam, a few high-yield questions, and documentation. That should help residents separate true hypertensive emergencies from patients who just need repeat vitals, med reconciliation, maybe oral adjustment, and likely discharge from ED observation rather than admission. I do not want a giant automatic panel tied to every severe blood pressure reading.
turns.utterance: One thing that seems straightforward is starting with a quick BARKH screen up front, so the team can rapidly separate the true emergencies from the patients who mainly need reassessment and outpatient-oriented medication planning. And for some of that second group, an observation pathway may make more sense than jumping straight to admission.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—if we build the BARKH screen into the EHR with structured prompts and linked supporting orders, we can make sure nobody misses renal labs, ECG, or the basic documentation before treatment decisions. I especially want something that reduces ad hoc IV pushes given before anyone has documented target-organ assessment. Symptom-based should still have a reliable minimum floor.
turns.utterance: I think a BARKH screen would work really well if we can standardize the initial prompts and the supporting pieces around it, so nothing important gets missed before treatment decisions are made. That would fit nicely with a symptom-based algorithm and give people a consistent starting point.

turns.inner_thought: I need to say this clearly without sounding like I’m trying to skip care. Headache by itself is not a reason for broad emergency testing if the story and exam are otherwise reassuring. The branch point should be whether there are concerning findings suggesting brain, aorta, heart, kidneys, or retina—not the number and not generic discomfort. If I can get that principle into the pathway, we’ll stop overworking low-yield cases.
turns.utterance: Right, and I’d want the algorithm to be symptom-driven enough that a headache without concerning findings doesn’t automatically set off a broad emergency workup, whereas focal deficits, chest pain, pulmonary edema, or clues to kidney injury clearly would. That’s the distinction I think we need to teach better.

turns.inner_thought: I’m hearing the same high-level idea, but I still want a standard minimum assessment once a severe blood pressure presentation is identified. Then the symptom-based branching can guide whether we’re in a neuro, cardiac, renal, or vascular lane and which meds and monitoring rules apply. The key for me is not leaving the baseline evaluation up to individual variation when high-risk medications may be used.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I could see the pathway identifying the severe blood pressure presentation and then guiding a standard minimum assessment before branching medications and monitoring based on whether the picture seems more neurologic, cardiac, renal, or vascular. That still keeps it symptom-based, but gives the team a stable framework.

turns.inner_thought: Observation is where we can really reduce unnecessary admissions: keep them in ED obs, repeat pressures, re-examine, tweak oral meds, see if symptoms settle, and discharge if no BARKH injury emerges. I’m thinking of the many patients who currently get admitted just because everyone feels uneasy about the blood pressure number. This needs to be a practical alternative to inpatient telemetry for the non-emergency group.
turns.utterance: And I do think an observation pathway could help us keep a lot of these patients out of unnecessary admissions. If we have a clear lane for serial blood pressure checks, repeat exams, and medication adjustment, that gives clinicians somewhere reasonable to put people while the picture declares itself.

turns.inner_thought: Observation would also be a very useful controlled space after IV antihypertensive treatment starts, especially if we define nursing parameters and reassessment intervals. I’m thinking monitored holding after bolus or infusion while deciding whether the patient stabilizes enough for step-down versus ICU. If observation gets built in, I want it to support medication safety as much as bed stewardship.
turns.utterance: I like the observation idea. Having clear nursing parameters there would also help when patients receive IV antihypertensives and need a monitored period before their final bed is decided. It could make that handoff a lot cleaner.

turns.inner_thought: This is also a culture problem. Residents still say 'hypertensive urgency' and then act as though they’ve identified a time-sensitive disease when what they really have is a high number without organ injury. I want the language change to affect triage thinking, workup thresholds, and disposition—not just the academic framing. If they think BARKH first, they’ll stop reflexively admitting or treating the cuff reading.
turns.utterance: One of my bigger goals here is to stop residents from reflexively labeling these cases as urgency or crisis and instead have them think in terms of whether BARKH injury is present and what that means for disposition. If we can make that the mental model, I think a lot of downstream decisions get better.

turns.inner_thought: For next week, the easiest sell is a straw-man that preserves the current order-set skeleton and monitoring logic, but updates it with BARKH language, symptom-based branching, and an observation option. That gives the group something implementable right away without rebuilding triage from scratch. If the clinicians agree, I can turn that into an EHR revision pretty quickly.
turns.utterance: That sounds like a good way to frame it for the larger group. Maybe for next week we bring a straw-man pathway that keeps the current order-set skeleton but layers in BARKH language, symptom-based branching, and an observation option. Then we can see where people want to tighten or simplify it.
